title: Caribou Analysis and Modelling
text:
Introduction
Caribou play an important role for LFN, serving as a keystone species in local ecosystems and having cultural significance for Indigenous communities. Ecologically, caribou contribute to the health of boreal forests by influencing vegetation patterns and providing food for predators. Culturally, caribou provide food, materials for clothing and tools, and are a central part of local traditions and knowledge. Consequently, the conservation of their seasonal ranges, including winter foraging grounds and summer calving and grazing areas, is important for the health and long-term persistence of the population. However, these habitats are increasingly threatened by human activities and disturbances, particularly large-scale resource development like mining, which leads to habitat fragmentation and landscape alteration.
The establishment of Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs) and other protected lands are important tools for ensuring the long-term survival of caribou populations, as they allow for the management of these threats. These areas enable collaborative stewardship, respect traditional ecological knowledge, and support sustainable use, thus contributing to the persistence of caribou and their habitats. By prioritizing both ecological integrity and cultural continuity, IPCAs can thus strengthen conservation and sustainable land management now and in the future. As part of this project, we will evaluate the contribution of the proposed IPCAs to seasonal movements, habitat selection, and landscape connectivity.


Northern mountain caribou
There are 26 herds of Northern Mountain caribou in Yukon occupying most of the south and central regions (Environment Yukon 2016). Twelve of the herds intersect the LFN area of interest (Figure 1), with four herds crossing over into British Columbia (Swan Lake, Little Rancheria, Horseranch, and Liard Plateau). Each herd is managed based on its unique range and population characteristics (Ref). Population monitoring relies on aerial surveys and long-term data to assess herd status, recruitment (calf survival), and sex ratios.

title: Little Rancheria
text:
The conservation of migratory ungulates has undergone a paradigm shift from the protection of discrete seasonal ranges toward a holistic approach that prioritizes the continuity of the pathways connecting them. In the temperate and arid regions of the world, hooved mammals frequently undertake expansive journeys to synchronize their nutritional needs with the phenological “green wave” of emerging vegetation or to seek refuge from extreme winter conditions.1 These movements, which often span hundreds of kilometers across heterogeneous landscapes, are increasingly threatened by the accelerating pace of anthropogenic fragmentation, including expansive road networks, energy infrastructure, and the proliferation of fencing.1 Consequently, the development of sophisticated statistical and computational tools to identify, map, and prioritize these seasonal corridors has become a cornerstone of modern wildlife management and landscape ecology. The period between 2020 and 2026 has been marked by a significant escalation in the refinement of these methodologies, catalyzed by high-resolution telemetry, global collaborative initiatives, and the integration of machine learning into ecological modeling.4


The systemic identification of ungulate corridors has evolved from localized studies into large-scale institutional endeavors. In the United States, a pivotal moment occurred in 2018 with the establishment of Secretarial Order 3362, which provided the federal mandate and financial support required to expand research on big game winter ranges and migration corridors across the Western states.4 This order facilitated the formation of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Corridor Mapping Team (CMT), a massive collaboration involving eleven state agencies, regional and federal partners, and an increasing number of Tribal wildlife agencies.6 The CMT’s primary contribution is a standardized analytical framework that enables the synthesis of movement data from thousands of GPS-collared animals into a unified, map-based inventory.4
By February 2025, the CMT had reached a milestone with the publication of the fifth volume of the “Ungulate Migrations of the Western United States” report series, bringing the total number of unique ungulate herds mapped to 218.4 This inventory is critical because it moves beyond the traditional perception of migration as a single, well-defined line. Instead, it recognizes that temperate ungulates often utilize summer ranges significantly larger than their winter ranges, necessitating a complex network of multiple routes used by different segments of a population.7 The reports provide technical details and visually engaging maps that identify “low,” “medium,” and “high” use areas, as well as critical stopover sites where animals spend roughly 95% of their time during the migration period to forage and recover energy.6

Parallel to the USGS efforts, the Global Initiative for Ungulate Migration (GIUM), established in 2020, launched the first interactive UN Atlas of Ungulate Migration.11 This global tool tracks the movements of large land mammals such as zebras, Mongolian gazelles, and Alpine ibex in real-time. The emergence of these platforms signifies a transition toward “actionable science,” where migration data is no longer siloed in academic journals but is directly accessible to policymakers and infrastructure planners to guide the placement of wildlife overpasses and the modification of deer-friendly fencing.1



At the core of corridor identification is the challenge of converting discrete GPS locations—points in time and space—into continuous probability distributions of use. The historical reliance on simple “connect-the-dots” lines or static home-range estimators has been largely superseded by models that account for the spatial and temporal uncertainty of an animal’s path.7
The Brownian Bridge Movement Model (BBMM) has emerged as the definitive statistical framework for mapping seasonal corridors.2 The BBMM treats the movement between two successive locations as a conditional random walk, or a “bridge,” where the probability of occurrence is highest along the direct path and expands laterally based on the time elapsed and the animal’s mobility.7 This approach is particularly powerful because it generates a utilization distribution (UD), which characterizes the population-level route network rather than just individual tracks.7
A critical insight gained from BBMM applications is the functional differentiation within a migration route. Analyses of mule deer in southwest Wyoming, for instance, have delineated a series of high-use stopover sites connected by movement corridors through which animals pass quickly.8 Stopovers are characterized by specific habitat attributes: south-southwesterly aspects, low elevation, and high-quality early spring forage.15 By prioritizing these stopovers, managers can protect the “energy stations” that allow ungulates to sustain long-distance movements.6
The precision of BBMMs, however, is inextricably linked to the sampling frequency of GPS collars. Traditional BBMMs require location data sampled at relatively frequent intervals—typically every one to three hours—to provide a robust estimate of the path.2 When data are sparse, such as locations taken every 12 to 26 hours, the BBMM tends to violate the assumption of conditional random movement, leading to an overestimation of the corridor’s width and area.14 This “inflation” can be detrimental to conservation efforts, as overly wide corridors may include irrelevant land, making them difficult to protect legally or include in highway mitigation plans.2



In many real-world scenarios, wildlife managers must rely on sparse data due to the high costs of frequent GPS fixes or the need to preserve battery life for long-term monitoring.12 To bridge this gap, recent research has introduced the Fixed Motion Variance (FMV) approach to the BBMM framework.13 By constraining the Brownian motion variance () to a fixed, species-specific value rather than estimating it empirically from sparse data, models can more accurately approximate the narrow dimensions of actual migration paths.14
Validation studies using mule deer and elk herds in Idaho and Wyoming have demonstrated that optimal FMV values can reduce corridor area inflation by over 50%.13 These findings have established species-specific benchmarks that allow for the retroactive analysis of legacy datasets, effectively expanding the volume of trackable herds that can be used for corridor mapping.13

Beyond mapping where an animal has been, there is a growing necessity to predict where animals will migrate, particularly in areas where populations are uncollared or where corridors have been disrupted and require restoration.1 This has led to the development of predictive cost-distance models. Unlike older habitat suitability models that required the subjective transformation of habitat layers into resistance surfaces, modern statistical frameworks use maximum likelihood and optimization to directly estimate how environmental factors—such as elevation, slope, and human footprint—influence the “cost” of movement.1 These models function similarly to wayfinding apps, identifying the best route between seasonal ranges based on rules that balance energy expenditure with forage access.1


While BBMMs are descriptive, researchers seeking to understand the underlying behavioral mechanisms of corridor selection utilize Step-Selection Functions (SSF). The SSF framework is designed to link environmental covariates to location data collected at fine temporal resolutions, providing a mechanistic look at how animals choose their path.18
A significant advancement in this area is the Integrated Step-Selection Analysis (iSSA), which simultaneously models both movement (step length and turning angle) and habitat selection.18 By comparing the “used” steps of an animal to a set of “available” random steps, iSSAs can reveal complex trade-offs, such as how ungulates might balance the ease of travel on a road with the risk of human interaction.23 The mathematical likelihood of an animal selecting a specific location  at time  is modeled as:

In cases where individual movement data is absent, or to evaluate the structural connectivity of an entire landscape, practitioners employ connectivity modeling software. These tools generally fall into two categories: those based on least-cost paths and those based on circuit theory.25
Linkage Mapper is a primary tool for drawing “least-cost paths” between defined habitat cores.26 It operates on the assumption that animals have perfect knowledge of the landscape and will always take the most efficient route.26 While this is a simplification of animal behavior, it is highly effective for identifying the structural backbone of a corridor network.25 Circuitscape, conversely, utilizes algorithms from electrical circuit theory to simulate movement as a flow of current across a resistance surface.27 This allows for the identification of multiple potential pathways and redundant corridors, making it particularly useful for finding “pinch points” or bottlenecks where connectivity is most vulnerable to development.26
The evolution of these tools has led to Omniscape, which provides an “omnidirectional” circuit-theoretic approach.26 Unlike its predecessors, Omniscape does not require the pre-definition of habitat cores (point A to point B). Instead, it treats every pixel on the landscape as a potential target, calculating possible paths in every direction to produce a wall-to-wall heatmap of connectivity.26 This is vital for assessing how broad landscapes might support range shifts under the pressure of climate change.26

The integration of artificial intelligence represents the latest frontier in corridor mapping, specifically in the use of deep sequence models and automated object detection.30 Traditional parametric models often struggle with the non-linear dependencies of long-term migration trajectories. Deep learning architectures, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), have demonstrated a superior ability to predict the next location of a migratory animal by analyzing spatio-temporal sequences.30 BiLSTMs are notably effective as they process data in both forward (past to present) and backward (future to present) directions, capturing a deeper context of the animal’s movement intent.32
In the realm of remote sensing, high-density LiDAR (light detection and ranging) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are being used to map physical trails and tracks in dense forests.33 In the Canadian boreal forest, this workflow revealed a massive 2,829-km network of trails within a 59-km² area—features that were previously invisible to traditional satellite imagery.33 These studies have shown that wildlife are significantly funneled by linear industrial disturbances, such as seismic lines, which creates a “movement superhighway” for predators and alters the natural dynamics of the ecosystem.33
Similarly, in Kruger National Park, drone-based RGB orthomosaics analyzed via the UNet deep learning architecture have achieved an 83% accuracy rate in automatically detecting animal path systems.34 This “collar-less” approach offers a scalable way to identify movement corridors in data-poor environments and provides a spatially continuous view of route networks that discrete GPS pings cannot capture.34



A critical challenge for the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework is the design of corridors that support multiple species with diverse requirements.35 Multi-species connectivity (MSC) analyses aim to identify a network of habitats that supports the long-term persistence of an entire metacommunity rather than a single focal species.35
A common strategy in MSC is the use of “proxy” species. In savanna ecosystems, zebra have been identified as a robust proxy for broader ungulate connectivity, as their movement models show high correlation with species like wildebeest and gazelles.37 However, the effectiveness of a proxy is highly site-specific; for instance, elephants often serve as poor proxies for smaller ungulate community movements in African landscapes.37 New frameworks, such as the one tested on 193 species in France, cluster animals into groups based on shared environmental traits—such as body size and habitat sensitivity—to provide a more nuanced and realistic assessment of landscape connectivity.36

The future of corridor mapping lies in the synthesis of these multi-species models with real-time data and explainable AI (XAI).32 By revealing the specific factors that influence model predictions—such as temperature, snow depth, or human activity—XAI can provide ecological insights that go beyond simple spatial mapping.32 This transparency is essential for building the public and political trust required to implement large-scale corridor protection, such as the designating of three new mule deer migration corridors in Wyoming under HB 39.1



The review of current methods for identifying seasonal movement corridors indicates that a multi-tiered approach is most effective. The foundational mapping should utilize Brownian Bridge Movement Models, optimized with Fixed Motion Variance in cases of sparse data, to delineate high-use corridors and stopovers.13 These descriptive maps should then be complemented by mechanistic models like integrated step-selection functions to understand the environmental drivers of movement.18 For predictive and structural connectivity, tools like Circuitscape and Omniscape offer a robust way to identify “pinch points” and statewide connectivity patterns.26
The rapid advancement of machine learning and remote sensing—specifically LiDAR-based trail detection and LSTM-based trajectory prediction—is providing the next generation of tools to map “continuous” movement networks.32 As global initiatives like the GIUM continue to standardize and share this data, the primary hurdle remains the integration of these scientific outputs into the earliest stages of infrastructure planning and policy.1 The comprehensive mapping of over 200 herds in the Western U.S. serves as a global model for how collaborative, evidence-based science can lead to tangible conservation outcomes for the world’s migratory ungulates.4

text:
The concept of an animal’s home range, defined as the area traversed by an individual during its normal activities of food gathering, mating, and caring for young, forms a cornerstone of ecological research.1 Understanding the spatial extent and patterns of animal movement is crucial for addressing a wide array of ecological questions, including habitat use, social interactions, population dynamics, and conservation strategies.8 In an era marked by increasing human impact on natural environments, the ability to accurately delineate and analyze home ranges is more critical than ever, informing management decisions aimed at mitigating human-wildlife conflicts and ensuring the persistence of biodiversity.8
While the basic idea of a home range is intuitive, its quantification presents considerable challenges. Animals rarely utilize their environment uniformly; instead, they exhibit varying intensities of space use across their range. Isopleths, defined as lines connecting points of equal value, have emerged as a powerful tool in spatial ecology to address this complexity.11 In the context of home range estimation, isopleths provide a probabilistic framework for understanding the likelihood of an animal’s presence within a given area. This report aims to provide a comprehensive and expert-level analysis of isopleth levels in home range estimation. It will delve into the definition and role of isopleths, the interpretation of different probability levels, the common methods used to generate them, their applications in ecological analysis, and the crucial limitations and considerations that researchers must be aware of when employing this technique.

section: 2. Defining Isopleths in Home Range Estimation
text:
2. Defining Isopleths in Home Range Estimation
In ecological studies and wildlife research, an isopleth is a contour line drawn on a map that connects points representing an equal probability density of an animal’s location.11 These lines are not arbitrary; they are derived from an underlying statistical representation of an animal’s space use known as the utilization distribution (UD).1 The UD essentially maps the relative frequency with which an animal is found in different parts of its environment over a specific period, thereby quantifying the intensity of space use.
The concept of the UD can be visualized as a three-dimensional surface draped over the landscape, where the height of the surface at any given point corresponds to the probability density of the animal being located there. The total volume under this surface is normalized to sum to 1, representing the total probability of the animal being somewhere within its range.11 Isopleths are then the two-dimensional contours formed by slicing this three-dimensional probability surface at different height levels, corresponding to different probabilities of occurrence. These contours delineate areas within which there is a specified probability of finding the animal.
This probabilistic approach offered by isopleths stands in stark contrast to earlier, more simplistic methods of home range estimation, such as the Minimum Convex Polygon (MCP).1 While the MCP method simply connects the outermost recorded locations of an animal to form a polygon, it provides no information about how the animal uses the space within that boundary. Isopleths, by being derived from the UD, offer a much more nuanced understanding of space use, revealing areas of high and low intensity of activity and allowing for a probabilistic interpretation of an animal’s spatial behavior.

3. The Role of Isopleths in Delineating Home Ranges
Isopleths serve as the operational tool for defining the spatial extent of an animal’s home range by allowing researchers to select a specific probability level that corresponds to their definition of the range.1 For instance, a researcher might choose the 95% isopleth to represent the overall home range, implying that there is a 95% probability of finding the animal within the area enclosed by this contour at any given time.
Different isopleth levels can delineate distinct zones of space use intensity within the broader home range.1 For example, the 50% isopleth is commonly used to identify the core area, representing the region where the animal spends the majority of its time or has the highest probability of being located. Conversely, higher percentage isopleths encompass progressively larger areas that include the less frequently visited parts of the home range.
The selection of the isopleth level used to define the home range boundary is a critical decision that can significantly influence the estimated size and shape of the range.11 This choice should not be arbitrary but rather should be guided by the specific ecological question being addressed and the biological characteristics of the species under investigation. For example, a study focusing on resource acquisition might prioritize the core area defined by a lower isopleth, while a study on dispersal patterns might be more interested in the overall extent defined by a higher isopleth.
Furthermore, isopleths provide a standardized and quantitative way to compare home range characteristics between individuals, populations, or across different temporal scales.1 By comparing the areas enclosed by isopleths at the same probability level (e.g., 95%) for different animals, researchers can assess differences in home range size. Similarly, analyzing the degree of overlap between isopleths of different individuals can provide insights into social interactions and territoriality.


4. Understanding Different Isopleth Levels and Their Probabilistic Interpretation
Different isopleth levels represent different probabilities of an animal’s location within its home range. Understanding these probabilities is crucial for interpreting ecological patterns and processes.
50% Isopleth: The 50% isopleth delineates the area where there is a 50% probability of finding the animal at any random point in time within the study period.11 Ecologically, this is commonly interpreted as the core area of an animal’s home range, representing the zone of most intensive use. This area likely encompasses key resources, such as primary foraging sites, crucial resting locations, or important areas for social interactions.11 For instance, comparisons of core area size and location can reveal differences in resource availability or social status among individuals.
90% or 95% Isopleth: These higher-level isopleths, typically the 90% or 95% contours, are generally used to represent the overall home range extent.1 The 95% isopleth, for example, indicates the area within which there is a 95% probability of finding the animal. These levels capture the total area an animal regularly uses, including both the intensively used core and the more peripheral areas that may be visited less frequently for exploration or accessing seasonally available resources. While 95% is a common standard, some researchers advocate for the use of the 90% isopleth in specific contexts.1
Other isopleth levels, such as 75% or 99%, can also be used depending on the specific research objectives.13 For instance, a 75% isopleth might be used to define a secondary area of high use, while a 99% isopleth could represent the maximum extent of occasional excursions.
It is also important to understand the concept of “percent volume contours” in the context of three-dimensional utilization distributions.11 A 2D isopleth at a given percentage can be thought of as the projection of the corresponding volume contour from the 3D UD onto a two-dimensional map. This means that the area enclosed by an isopleth represents a specific proportion of the total probability volume of the animal’s space use.
Ultimately, the choice of which isopleth levels to analyze and interpret should be driven by the specific ecological questions being asked and the biological characteristics of the study animal.1 Relying solely on arbitrary conventions like always using the 50% and 95% isopleths without considering their ecological relevance to the species and the study system can lead to misleading interpretations.

5. Common Methods for Generating Home Range Isopleths
Several methods are commonly employed to generate isopleths for home range estimation, each with its own underlying assumptions and computational approaches.
Kernel Density Estimation (KDE): Kernel Density Estimation is one of the most widely used non-parametric methods for estimating an animal’s utilization distribution from a set of location data.1 The fundamental principle of KDE involves placing a kernel function, which is a probability density function (often a bivariate normal distribution), centered at each observed location of the animal.17 These individual kernels are then summed across all locations to produce an overall estimate of the probability density of the animal’s presence at any given point in space.
A critical aspect of KDE is the selection of the bandwidth or smoothing parameter.13 The bandwidth determines the size and shape of the kernel and significantly influences the resulting UD and the derived isopleths. A small bandwidth results in a highly localized and potentially fragmented UD, reflecting fine-scale movements, while a large bandwidth produces a smoother, more generalized UD that may obscure important details. Several methods exist for bandwidth selection, including least-squares cross-validation (LSCV) and plug-in methods, but the choice often involves a degree of subjectivity and can substantially impact the results.19
KDE offers several advantages, including its ability to estimate complex, non-linear home range shapes that are not constrained by convexity, and its provision of a continuous utilization distribution from which isopleths at any desired probability level can be extracted.5 However, KDE also has limitations. It is sensitive to the choice of bandwidth, can potentially overestimate home range size, particularly for animals with linear movement patterns or home ranges containing large areas of unused space.16 Furthermore, traditional KDE assumes that the location data are statistically independent, an assumption that is often violated by GPS telemetry data which typically exhibit temporal autocorrelation.19
Minimum Convex Polygon (MCP): The Minimum Convex Polygon is a more traditional and geometrically straightforward method for home range estimation.1 It defines the home range as the smallest convex polygon that encloses all the recorded locations of an animal. While a 100% MCP includes all data points, variations exist, such as the 95% MCP, which excludes a small percentage (typically 5%) of the most outlying locations to reduce the influence of occasional excursions.
While isopleths derived from UDs represent probability densities, MCPs essentially define a boundary based on the outermost occurrences. However, one can conceptually link MCPs to isopleths by considering polygons that enclose a specific percentage of the data points.
The primary advantages of MCP are its simplicity in calculation and interpretation.19 Its historical prevalence also allows for comparisons with older studies.20 However, MCP suffers from significant limitations. It tends to overestimate home range size, often including large areas that are rarely or never used by the animal.6 It is also highly sensitive to the inclusion of even a single outlying location, which can disproportionately inflate the estimated range. Critically, MCP provides no information about the intensity of space use within the defined polygon.16
Local Convex Hull (LoCoH): Local Convex Hull is a non-parametric kernel method that offers an alternative to traditional KDE, particularly for home ranges with complex shapes.1 LoCoH constructs a series of overlapping local convex hulls based on subsets of the animal’s location data. These subsets are typically defined by a fixed number of nearest neighbors (k-LoCoH), a fixed radius around each point (r-LoCoH), or an adaptive radius based on the distance to neighboring points (a-LoCoH).
Utilization distributions and isopleths can be derived from the density of these overlapping local hulls.65 LoCoH offers advantages in its ability to better represent home ranges with intricate boundaries, including those with internal unused areas or “hard” boundaries such as coastlines or rivers.1 Research suggests that LoCoH may provide more accurate estimates and exhibit better convergence properties as sample size increases compared to parametric KDE methods.1
Other Methods: Beyond KDE, MCP, and LoCoH, several other methods exist for home range estimation that can generate utilization distributions and, consequently, isopleths. These include:

Brownian Bridge Movement Models (BBMM): These models explicitly incorporate the animal’s movement path and the temporal autocorrelation between consecutive locations, making them well-suited for analyzing GPS tracking data.1
Autocorrelated Kernel Density Estimation (aKDE): This is a modification of traditional KDE that accounts for the temporal autocorrelation inherent in many animal tracking datasets, providing more robust estimates for serially correlated locations.1
Time-Geographic Density Estimation (TGDE): This approach generates a continuous probability density surface of an animal’s movements by considering both the spatial locations and the time elapsed between them, incorporating constraints on the animal’s maximum velocity.32
Density-based Fuzzy Home Range Estimator (DFHRE): This novel method aims to improve home range estimation by incorporating environmental factors such as terrain and obstacles, which can influence animal movement and space use.66

6. Interpretation and Application of Isopleth Levels in Ecological Analysis
Isopleth levels are invaluable tools for interpreting and analyzing animal space use in various ecological contexts.
Identifying Core Areas of Activity: The 50% isopleth is a widely adopted standard for delineating the core area of an animal’s home range.11 This area of highest probability of use often reflects the locations of essential resources or habitats that are critical for the animal’s survival and reproduction.11 Researchers can use the 50% isopleth to identify key foraging sites, important resting locations, or areas crucial for social interactions. Comparing the size, shape, and location of core areas across individuals or under different environmental conditions can provide insights into resource competition, habitat quality, or the impact of disturbances.
Defining the Overall Home Range Extent: Higher isopleth levels, typically 90% or 95%, are used to estimate the total spatial extent of an animal’s home range.1 This provides a measure of the total area an animal regularly utilizes, including both the core and the less frequently visited peripheral regions. Understanding the overall home range extent is crucial for conservation planning, as it helps determine the amount of habitat required to support individuals or populations. It can also be important for studying dispersal patterns and potential interactions with human activities or landscape features.8
Comparing Space Use Patterns: Isopleths at different probability levels offer a valuable tool for comparing space use patterns among individuals, between populations, or across different time periods or environmental conditions.2 For instance, comparing the 50% isopleths of two individuals might reveal differences in their core resource areas, while comparing their 95% isopleths could indicate variations in overall range size. Furthermore, changes in isopleth size or location over time can reflect responses to changes in resource availability, the presence of competitors or predators, or habitat alterations.11 Overlap indices, calculated using the utilization distributions from which isopleths are derived, provide quantitative measures of the degree of spatial overlap between individuals or groups.1
Analyzing Habitat Selection and Resource Utilization: By overlaying isopleth maps with spatial data on habitat types, resource distribution, or other environmental variables, researchers can analyze habitat selection patterns within different zones of space use intensity.7 For example, comparing the proportion of different habitat types within the 50% isopleth (core area) to that within the 95% isopleth (overall range) can reveal whether an animal exhibits specific habitat preferences in its most intensively used areas.17 This can provide valuable insights into the factors driving habitat selection and resource use.
Visualizing Intensity of Use: Isopleth maps offer a powerful visual representation of the intensity with which an animal utilizes its space across its home range.7 The spacing of isopleth lines indicates the gradient of use intensity; closely spaced lines signify a rapid change in the probability of occurrence, while widely spaced lines suggest a more gradual transition. This visual representation can be crucial for communicating research findings and understanding the spatial ecology of a species.


7. Limitations and Considerations When Using Isopleth Levels
While isopleth levels are a valuable tool in home range analysis, it is crucial to be aware of their limitations and to consider several factors when interpreting and applying them.
The influence of sample size and data collection methods cannot be overstated.5 The accuracy and reliability of home range estimates, and consequently the derived isopleths, are directly dependent on having a sufficient number of location data points that are representative of the animal’s space use over the relevant time period.13 Insufficient data can lead to underestimation or misrepresentation of the home range. Furthermore, the method of data collection, such as GPS telemetry versus VHF radio telemetry, can introduce biases due to factors like location accuracy, fix rates, and potential for signal obstruction.5
Spatial and temporal autocorrelation in animal tracking data pose a significant challenge for many traditional home range estimation methods, including standard Kernel Density Estimation.4 The non-independence of consecutive location points, where points closer in time are likely to be closer in space, violates the assumption of independence underlying these methods. This can lead to biased estimates of home range size and shape. Researchers should consider using methods specifically designed to address autocorrelation, such as Autocorrelated Kernel Density Estimation (aKDE) or Brownian Bridge Movement Models (BBMM).1
The subjectivity in parameter selection for certain home range estimation methods is another important consideration.15 For instance, the choice of bandwidth in KDE can significantly influence the resulting utilization distribution and isopleths, and different bandwidth selection methods can yield varying outcomes.15 Similarly, parameters in other methods like LoCoH (e.g., the number of neighbors) can also affect the results.41 Researchers should be aware of this subjectivity and, where possible, justify their parameter choices based on ecological knowledge or employ sensitivity analyses to assess the impact of different parameter values.
Different home range estimation methods have inherent biases and assumptions that can affect the interpretation of isopleth levels.1 For example, MCPs are known to overestimate home range size, while traditional KDE might smooth over important fine-scale patterns or extend into areas that are physically inaccessible to the animal.6 The choice of method should be carefully considered in relation to the specific characteristics of the animal’s movement and the research question.
The selection of appropriate isopleth levels is crucial for meaningful ecological interpretation.1 Relying on arbitrary conventions like always using 50% and 95% isopleths without considering their ecological relevance to the species and the study system can lead to misleading conclusions.24 The choice should be driven by the specific research question and the biological significance of those levels for the animal under study.
Finally, standard home range estimation methods may not adequately account for environmental barriers and habitat heterogeneity.14 For example, a traditional KDE might produce isopleths that extend across a large river that the animal cannot cross. Newer methods, such as those incorporating cost distance or network-based approaches, can help address these limitations.16 Additionally, the heterogeneity of the habitat can influence space use patterns, and researchers should consider how this might be reflected in the shape and size of isopleths.7


8. Conclusion
Isopleth levels represent a sophisticated and valuable tool in the field of spatial ecology for understanding how animals utilize their environment. By providing a probabilistic framework for delineating home ranges and visualizing the intensity of space use, isopleths offer significant advantages over simpler methods. They enable researchers to identify core areas of activity, estimate overall home range extent, compare space use patterns across different groups or conditions, and analyze habitat selection within varying intensity-of-use zones.
However, the effective and responsible application of isopleth levels requires a thorough understanding of the underlying principles of home range estimation methods, as well as a critical awareness of their inherent limitations and assumptions. Factors such as sample size, data collection techniques, spatial and temporal autocorrelation, subjectivity in parameter selection, and the influence of environmental barriers must be carefully considered to ensure the generation of reliable and ecologically meaningful home range estimates. The selection of appropriate isopleth levels should be driven by the specific research questions and the biological characteristics of the species under investigation, rather than relying on arbitrary conventions.
In conclusion, isopleth analysis remains a cornerstone of ecological and wildlife research, providing essential insights into animal space use. By employing these techniques thoughtfully and with a clear understanding of their strengths and weaknesses, researchers can continue to advance our knowledge of animal behavior, population ecology, and the spatial dynamics of species in a changing world.

text:
Introduction
Caribou play an important role for LFN, serving as a keystone species in local ecosystems and having cultural significance for Indigenous communities. Ecologically, caribou contribute to the health of boreal forests by influencing vegetation patterns and providing food for predators. Culturally, caribou provide food, materials for clothing and tools, and are a central part of local traditions and knowledge. Consequently, the conservation of their seasonal ranges, including winter foraging grounds and summer calving and grazing areas, is important for the health and long-term persistence of the population. However, these habitats are increasingly threatened by human activities and disturbances, particularly large-scale resource development like mining, which leads to habitat fragmentation and landscape alteration.
The establishment of Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs) and other protected lands are important tools for ensuring the long-term survival of caribou populations, as they allow for the management of these threats. These areas enable collaborative stewardship, respect traditional ecological knowledge, and support sustainable use, thus contributing to the persistence of caribou and their habitats. By prioritizing both ecological integrity and cultural continuity, IPCAs can thus strengthen conservation and sustainable land management now and in the future. As part of this project, we will evaluate the contribution of the proposed IPCAs to seasonal movements, habitat selection, and landscape connectivity.

Although the Yukon Government also provides definitions fpr spring and fall migration periods, we decided, due to the large variation in movement patterns, to identify seasonal migration periods for each individual for each year. To do this we used Net Squared Displacement (NSD) analysis combined with visual inspection of the spatial distribution of GPS locations using the BEACONs Movement Mapper app to identify spring and fall migration start and end dates for each individual in each year. Migration periods were defined as follows:

Spring migration: Movement from winter range to summer range (generally northeast direction), beginning when individuals depart the winter range and ending upon arrival at summer range
Fall migration: Movement from summer range to winter range (generally southwest direction), beginning when individuals depart the summer range and ending upon arrival at winter range



We used the Movement Mapper app to identify start and end dates for spring and fall migration periods for each individual in each year.

For each individual/year:

Visualize movement tracks on map with seasonal color coding
Review NSD vs. day-of-year plots
Identify migration periods using these criteria:

Spring migration start: First sustained increase in NSD (e.g., >20% increase maintained for >7 days)
Spring migration end: NSD plateau or reversal indicating arrival at summer range
Fall migration start: First sustained decrease in NSD from summer range
Fall migration end: NSD plateau indicating establishment on winter range

Adjust date sliders to refine start/end dates based on visual assessment
If clear spring and fall migrations exist: Record start/end dates for both periods
If no evidence of migration assign NA to migration dates
Document ambiguous cases with comments in the notes field


Notes:
The first challenge in mapping a migration is figuring out when an animal is actually migrating versus when it is simply living in its seasonal home range. An individual caribou might wander for several kilometres in its summer territory, but that isn’t the same as its focused, directional journey between seasons. To solve this, we can use analytical tool called Net Squared Displacement (NSD). In simple terms, NSD measures the straight-line distance an animal is from a fixed starting point, which is typically set near the beginning of the biological year (e.g., January 1) within the animal’s winter range, and then squares that value. When plotted on a graph over a full year, the NSD curve for a migrating animal reveals a distinct, three-phase pattern:

In the starting range: When an individual is settled in its winter or summer range, it stays relatively close to the starting point. The NSD value fluctuates a little but remains low, creating a relatively flat line on the graph.
During migration: As the individual begins its journey to its summer or winter range, it moves steadily away from the starting point. This causes the NSD value to increase sharply and consistently, creating a steep upward slope on the graph.
In the target range: Once the individual arrives and settles in its summer or winter range, it is far from the starting point, so the NSD value is high. However, because it is no longer moving in a single direction, the value stabilizes and flattens out again at this new, higher level.

The “clear breakpoints” on the graph – where the line begins to rise and where it flattens out – allow us to identify the exact start and end dates of the spring and fall migrations. All the locations recorded between these dates are then grouped together, forming a single “migration sequence” for that animal in that year.

Estimating the boundaries of seasonal and annual caribou ranges is an important step in effective wildlife conservation and management. Defining these spatial limits allows managers to identify core habitat areas, including calving grounds and winter foraging areas. This information is fundamental for land use planning, as it ensures that development and human activities are regulated to minimize disturbance and avoid habitat loss and fragmentation within these key areas. Ultimately, understanding and mapping caribou ranges provides the necessary baseline data to implement targeted conservation measures, monitor population health in relation to their environment, and support sustainable resource management for the long-term persistence of the herds.
We estimated annual and seasonal ranges using locations collected from many caribou over multiple years. To understand how herds use the landscape across the year, we grouped these locations into biologically meaningful seasons: annual, early winter, late winter, summer, and the fall rut. For each season, we used a statistical mapping approach called a kernel density estimator (KDE), implemented in R using the amt package. This method creates smooth contours around clusters of points, showing where caribou spend most of their time. The outer contour (the 95% isopleth) represents the broader seasonal range, while the inner contour (the 50% isopleth) highlights the core areas most heavily used.
This approach provides a consistent way to compare how different herds use space and how their ranges shift across seasons. Because it summarizes many individual movement paths into a single population‑level map, it helps identify key habitats and areas that may require conservation attention. The graphic below illustrates the concept, showing points, the estimated 95% range boundary, and the 50% core area for an example herd.
Individual-level range estimation
For each individual/year/season, use the Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) method to estimate probability density functions of animal locations, resulting in utilization distributions.
Parameters: Select appropriate smoothing parameters (e.g., h-value) using methods like Likelihood Cross-Validation (LCV) or reference bandwidth.
Output: Generate 95% and 50% (or other relevant contours) utilization distributions (UDs) for annual and seasonal ranges for each individual for each year. The former (95%) represents the overall annual or seasonal range while the latter (50% isopleths) represents core or high use areas.
Population-level range estimation
There are two broad approaches that could be used to estimate population-level annual and seasonal ranges:

Method 1 - Union of individual ranges: Combine individual ranges (e.g., 95% KDEs) to visualize the total area used by the population annually and seasonally.

Estimating the boundaries of seasonal and annual caribou ranges is an important step in effective wildlife conservation and management. Defining these spatial limits allows managers to identify core habitat areas, including calving grounds and winter foraging areas. This information is fundamental for land use planning, as it ensures that development and human activities are regulated to minimize disturbance and avoid habitat loss and fragmentation within these key areas. Ultimately, understanding and mapping caribou ranges provides the necessary baseline data to implement targeted conservation measures, monitor population health in relation to their environment, and support sustainable resource management for the long-term persistence of the herds.
We estimated annual and seasonal ranges using locations collected from many caribou over multiple years. To understand how herds use the landscape across the year, we grouped these locations into biologically meaningful seasons: annual, early winter, late winter, summer, and the fall rut. For each season, we used a statistical mapping approach called a kernel density estimator (KDE), implemented in R using the amt package. This method creates smooth contours around clusters of points, showing where caribou spend most of their time. The outer contour (the 95% isopleth) represents the broader seasonal range, while the inner contour (the 50% isopleth) highlights the core areas most heavily used.
This approach provides a consistent way to compare how different herds use space and how their ranges shift across seasons. Because it summarizes many individual movement paths into a single population‑level map, it helps identify key habitats and areas that may require conservation attention.
